issues.legal_issue: The filing of a charge sheet during the pendency of a petition to quash criminal proceedings does not prevent the court from considering whether those proceedings should be quashed.
material_facts: The accused had sought quashing of an FIR under the High Court’s inherent jurisdiction.
A charge sheet was filed while the challenge to the FIR was pending, and the accused also sought to quash the charge sheet.
issues.conclusion: The charge sheet did not make the challenge to the FIR untenable; the court could consider quashing both the FIR and the charge sheet.
issues.legal_principle: Section 482 of the Code of Criminal Procedure preserves the High Court’s inherent power to prevent abuse of process or secure the ends of justice, and its text does not confine that power to the FIR stage. In Joseph Salvaraj A. v. State of Gujarat, the Court held that a court may examine whether alleged offences are prima facie made out even when a charge sheet has been filed during the pendency of a quashing petition. The Court also referred to G. Sagar Suri v. State of U.P. and Umesh Kumar v. State of Andhra Pradesh for the settled principle that the power may be exercised even when a discharge application is pending before the trial court.

predicates.criminal_proceeding_challenged_under_inh: A person asks a court to use its inherent power to stop a criminal proceeding.
predicates.quashing_petition_pending: The request to quash the criminal proceeding remains pending before the court.
predicates.charge_sheet_filed_during_petition: A charge sheet is filed while the request to quash the proceeding is pending.

issues.definition: When a request to quash a criminal proceeding remains pending and a charge sheet is filed during that time, the court may still consider quashing the FIR and charge sheet.

issues.legal_issue: Transferring property belonging to an accused does not constitute criminal breach of trust when that property was not entrusted to the accused by the complainant.
material_facts: The property alleged to have been transferred belonged to one of the accused.
The complainant had entered into a development agreement concerning the property but had not entrusted the property to the accused.
issues.conclusion: The alleged transfer, even if unlawful, could not constitute criminal breach of trust because the property had not been entrusted to the accused by the complainant.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 405 and 406 of the Indian Penal Code require, among other things, that the accused be entrusted with property or dominion over it and dishonestly misappropriate, convert, use, or dispose of it in breach of the relevant direction or obligation. A person cannot be entrusted by a complainant with property that belongs to the accused merely because the parties have entered into an agreement concerning that property.

predicates.criminal_breach_of_trust_alleged: The complainant alleges that the accused committed criminal breach of trust by transferring property.
predicates.property_belonged_to_accused: The property allegedly transferred belonged to the accused.
predicates.complainant_did_not_entrust_property_to_: The complainant had not entrusted the property to the accused.

issues.definition: If a criminal breach of trust is alleged based on a transfer of the accused’s own property, but the complainant did not entrust that property to the accused, the alleged transfer does not establish criminal breach of trust.

issues.legal_issue: Criminal proceedings for breach of trust should be quashed when the alleged retention of a contractual deposit does not disclose dishonest use or misappropriation and the dispute is civil in nature.
material_facts: A developer paid an interest-free deposit under a development agreement.

The agreement provided for return of the deposit when the developer handed over the constructed area allocated to the owner, but that event had not occurred because the contemplated development had not taken place.
The accused said the deposit was retained as security, including because the complainant remained in part possession of the property and had not fulfilled related obligations.
The complainant maintained that the agreement remained in force and had not demanded return of the deposit; it made no attempt to recover the money through a civil action.

The FIR and charge sheet alleged breach of trust based on retention of the deposit, but the material did not show that the accused had dishonestly used or misappropriated it contrary to law or contract.
issues.conclusion: The dispute was civil in nature and did not disclose criminal breach of trust; the FIR and charge sheet were quashed as an abuse of process.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 405 and 406 of the Indian Penal Code require entrustment and dishonest misappropriation, conversion, use, or disposal of property contrary to a legal direction or contract. Under Section 482 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, proceedings may be quashed where the allegations, even taken at face value, do not prima facie constitute an offence, where uncontroverted allegations and collected evidence disclose no offence, or where the allegations are inherently improbable. State of Haryana v. Bhajan Lal identifies these categories for exercise of inherent power; State of Karnataka v. L. Muniswamy recognizes that proceedings may be quashed to prevent abuse or harassment. Indian Oil Corporation v. NEPC India Ltd. cautions against using criminal prosecution to pressure a party in a civil dispute. The Court also treated the absence of any attempt to recover the deposit through civil action as supporting its conclusion that the prosecution was mala fide.

rule.if: criminal_proceeding_over_contractual_deposit and deposit_paid_under_agreement and repayment_condition_not_occurred and no_dishonest_use_or_misappropriation and dispute_is_civil_in_nature

predicates.criminal_proceeding_over_contractual_dep: A criminal proceeding alleges breach of trust based on a party’s retention of a deposit paid under a contract.
predicates.deposit_paid_under_agreement: The complainant paid the disputed money as a deposit under an agreement.
predicates.repayment_condition_not_occurred: The contractual event that triggers return of the deposit has not occurred.
predicates.no_dishonest_use_or_misappropriation: The material does not show that the accused dishonestly used or misappropriated the deposit contrary to law or contract.
predicates.dispute_is_civil_in_nature: The dispute concerns contractual rights and obligations and does not disclose a criminal offence.

issues.definition: When a criminal proceeding over a contractual deposit concerns money paid under an agreement, the repayment condition has not occurred, dishonest use or misappropriation is not shown, and the dispute is civil in nature, the proceeding is quashed as an abuse of process.
